q: Your chatbot answers turn 2 as if turn 1 never happened. The code sends only the newest user message. What is the root cause?
options: The API is stateless, so history must be re-sent by the app
The model temperature is too low
The API key lacks conversation scope
why: Each request is independent; the app must include prior messages. Temperature and system prompt do not create memory.

q: Where should an LLM API key live in a web product?
options: In a server-side secret store or env var, with calls proxied by your backend
In the git repo, in a private branch
why: Client code is readable by users and git history persists. Obfuscation does not protect a bearer key; a backend proxy can also add auth and rate limits.

q: A response has finish_reason 'length'. What does this most likely mean and what do you do?
options: The prompt was too long; delete history
Output hit max tokens and was cut off; raise the limit or shorten the answer
why: 'length' signals truncation by the output cap. A refusal or content filter has different reasons; treating length as success silently ships cut-off answers.

q: Why is the full 200-turn chat log in your DB not simply sent every request?
options: Databases cannot be read by LLMs
Context is limited and costly, so you project only what the task needs
why: State and context are different: select recent turns, summaries and fresh facts. Storing the full log remains useful for audit and UI.

q: What does streaming primarily improve?
options: Time to first visible output and perceived responsiveness
why: Output rate is unchanged, so total time and cost are about the same; users just see text sooner.

q: During a streamed tool call, when should you parse the arguments JSON?
options: After the tool-call block completes and fragments are concatenated
why: Fragments are partial JSON and fail to parse early. Accumulate by id, then parse once complete.

q: A user closes the tab mid-answer, but provider bills keep growing. Fix?
options: Detect disconnect and abort the upstream stream
why: Without propagating cancellation the provider continues generating. Abort signals stop generation and cost.

q: You suspect LangChain is altering your prompt. Best first step?
options: Log/trace the final messages sent and replay them with the raw SDK
why: Seeing the exact request isolates whether the layer or the prompt/model is at fault.

q: What does `prompt | model | parser` primarily provide?
options: A composed runnable with shared invoke/stream/batch interface
A new model with better reasoning
why: The pipe composes runnables so streaming, batching and tracing work across stages. It does not alter model capability.

q: Which scenario most justifies a framework over the raw SDK?
options: Many providers and integrations with a team needing shared patterns
A latency-critical hot path with one call
why: Frameworks pay off when they remove significant repeated integration work; for tiny flows the abstraction mostly adds weight.

q: After swapping the model behind a common interface, outputs degrade. Most likely reason?
options: Prompts and defaults were tuned for the old model's behaviour
why: Same interface does not mean same behaviour; re-evaluate and retune prompts.

q: Which guarantee does JSON mode alone provide?
why: JSON mode ensures parseable JSON; fields and types may still differ from your schema, and truth is never guaranteed.

q: A classifier reports 100% schema-valid outputs but users complain of wrong labels. What does this show?
options: Schema validity says little about accuracy; evaluate semantic correctness
The schema is too loose only
why: Parse rate is a plumbing metric. Measure accuracy on labelled data and add grounding checks.

q: Output passes the schema: `{"discount_pct": 95}`. Policy caps discounts at 20. What should catch this?
options: A business-rule validation after schema validation
why: Type checks cannot enforce domain limits; add explicit rule validation before acting.

q: In a generate-validate-repair loop, what should the repair prompt include?
options: The original task, the invalid output and the specific validation error
why: Specific errors let the model fix the precise fault; blind retries repeat it.

q: Why make a field nullable in an extraction schema?
options: It reduces token cost to zero
So the model can say a value is absent instead of fabricating one
why: Forced required fields push the model to invent data when the source lacks it.

q: In function calling, who runs the function?
options: Your application, after the model emits a structured call
why: The model only produces the request; execution, validation and permissions are yours.

q: Why must each tool call receive a result message, even on failure?
options: APIs expect every call id answered and the model needs the failure info
why: Unanswered ids typically cause API errors and leave the model without information to recover.

q: Three independent lookups are requested in one response. Best handling?
options: Run sequentially, answering only the first
Run concurrently with timeouts and return all results by id
Merge them into one string with no ids
why: Independent calls can run concurrently to reduce latency; each result must be tied to its id.

q: A tool throws a timeout and your code returns [] . The bot says 'no records found'. The core mistake?
options: Failure disguised as an empty success
why: Return an explicit error or retry; empty results are read as true absence.

q: Two tools, `search_docs` and `find_documents`, are chosen at random. Best fix?
options: Merge them or sharpen descriptions with explicit usage boundaries
why: Overlap is a design flaw; clear, distinct scopes make selection reliable.

q: Which design best protects against prompt-injected tool arguments?
options: Server-side validation, authorisation from the session and confirmation for risky actions
why: Prompts can be bypassed; enforcement belongs in the tool layer.

q: Your assistant has 60 similar tools and selection accuracy is poor. Which is the most appropriate step?
options: Route or retrieve a relevant subset and consolidate duplicates
why: Reducing visible choices improves selection and cuts token cost; measure with an eval.

q: Why measure the token size of your tool definitions?
options: They are only used at deploy time
They are sent each request so they cost tokens, latency and attention
why: Tool schemas are part of the prompt and add to cost and context pressure.

q: Which task is best suited to a fixed workflow rather than an agent?
options: Extract fields, validate, then store in a database
Exploring a website to find an answer
why: Known steps favour workflows for predictability and cost; agents suit unknown, data-dependent paths.

q: A pipeline's final output is wrong and you cannot tell which step caused it. Best prevention?
options: Log and test intermediate outputs of each step
why: Step-level logging and tests localise faults; serialisable intermediates enable replay.

q: When is splitting a task into steps most clearly justified?
options: When an eval shows one sub-skill failing or steps need different models
why: Splits should be justified by measured quality, cost, size or verification needs, not preference.

q: Why does asyncio.gather speed up 100 independent LLM calls?
options: Calls mostly wait on network, so they overlap
why: I/O-bound waiting is overlapped; each call still costs the same tokens.

q: A semaphore around API calls is used primarily to:
options: Bound in-flight requests to stay within rate limits
why: Limiting concurrent calls prevents bursts that trigger 429s.

q: Nightly job to label 3M records with no deadline pressure within 24h. Best fit?
why: Batch APIs typically cost less and avoid rate-limit handling when latency is not needed.

q: Parallelism was doubled and cost per successful item rose. A plausible reason?
why: Excess parallelism can cause failures and retries that still consume resources; measure cost per success.

q: Which response should NOT be retried automatically?
options: Read timeout on a pure generation call
why: A context-length 400 will fail identically until the input changes. The others are transient.

q: Why add jitter to backoff delays?
options: To avoid many clients retrying simultaneously
why: Randomised delays spread load and prevent synchronized retry storms.

q: Where is the best place to implement timeouts and retries for all LLM calls?
options: One shared client wrapper or gateway
why: Central policy gives consistency and avoids multiplied retries across layers.

q: Your fallback model has never served traffic and fails during the outage. Best preventive practice?
options: Add more retries to the primary
Regularly test the fallback path with evals and synthetic traffic
why: Untested fallbacks often differ in tool support, prompt behavior or schema handling; exercise them before you need them.

q: A quality regression appears after a deploy. Which per-request field most directly lets you compare before/after?
options: Prompt template version and model id
why: Versioned prompts and model ids allow grouping outcomes by change.

q: The final answer is wrong; the trace shows retrieval returned irrelevant docs. Where should you fix first?
why: The generation step used bad context; fix upstream where the first wrong output appears.

q: Child tool-call spans appear as separate traces in async code. What is the usual cause?
options: Trace context not propagated across async tasks
why: Context must be carried across tasks/threads or spans lose their parent.

q: Which logging practice best supports debugging while respecting privacy?
options: Log every full prompt unredacted forever
Structured logs with ids, redaction and retained replay inputs for failures only
why: Structured, redacted, targeted retention gives debuggability without unnecessary exposure.

q: Which approach best fits an agent that must pause for human approval and resume later?
why: Persisted state and interrupts are core features of graph engines; chains lack resumability.

q: What does DSPy need to optimise a pipeline?
options: A dataset and a metric for scoring outputs
why: Optimisers search prompts or demos against a metric over examples; with neither, there is nothing to optimise.

q: A team picks a framework because it is popular, then struggles to debug hidden prompts. What process would have helped?
options: Prototyping with the raw SDK and trialling the library on one slice with an eval
why: Understanding the real work first and testing on a slice shows what the abstraction hides and whether it helps.

q: LlamaIndex is most associated with which concern?
options: Ingesting, indexing and retrieving over your data
why: Its core is the data-to-RAG pipeline: loaders, nodes, indexes, retrievers and query engines.

q: A client retries a timed-out chat call and the tool already charged the card. What was missing?
options: A request id created before attempt one and an idempotent tool
A higher temperature so the model is less likely to time out
A longer system prompt about being careful with payments
Switching to a cheaper model for retries
why: Timeouts still happen. The app must send a stable request id and tools must be idempotent so a retry does not double-charge.

q: Finance asks why last week's token bill jumped. You logged only response.content. What is missing?
options: The system prompt, which is the only billed field
Per-request usage (prompt, completion, cached) plus model id and finish reason
The raw API key so finance can open the vendor dashboard
why: Usage and model id are how you explain a bill. Content-only logs cannot reconstruct tokens or a finish_reason of length.

q: A streamed assistant message is shown to the user, but you never read the final finish reason. What bug slips through?
options: Truncated or tool-call streams are treated as complete answers
why: Streaming does not remove finish_reason. length and tool_calls still need a branch after the last delta.

q: The UI paints slowly so you buffer every stream delta in an unbounded list. What is the risk?
options: Memory grows with the response and a long answer can OOM the process
why: Slow consumers need backpressure or a bounded buffer. An unbounded stream in memory is a production incident.

q: A teammate says the LangChain model hallucinated. What correction do you make?
options: LangChain is the LLM, so swap the package
LangChain is an orchestration layer; the weights and the hidden prompt are still the model call
Parsers replace the need for a model
why: LangChain is a layer, not the model. Blame the rendered prompt and the provider call, not the import.

q: You swap providers behind a LangChain interface and lose retries and usage logs. What did you forget?
options: That frameworks hide the vendor; you still own retries, logging, and schemas
That only OpenAI can log usage
That parsers store the API key
why: A common interface is not a reliability layer. Retries, logs, and schemas stay yours after a vendor swap.

q: The model omits a required email field that your schema marked required. First recovery?
options: Accept the object and invent an email
Default in code if the product allows, or retry once with the validator error — then reject
Lower the required flag in production silently
why: Omitted required fields are a generate failure. One repair with the validator error, then reject. Do not invent PII.

q: A status field is a free-form string and the parser accepts 'n/a', 'N/A', and 'unknown'. What should the schema have used?
options: An enum (and optional/nullable if unknown is allowed) so the parser can trust the value
why: Tight types beat a free-form string. Enums and optional fields are how you stop synonym drift.

q: This turn must call refund_preview and must not chat first. Which tool_choice do you send?
options: auto, so the model can decline
required (or the named tool) so the turn cannot skip the call
Omit tool_choice; schemas force the call
why: auto can skip the tool. When the turn must call it, send required or the specific tool name.

q: You execute a tool but insert the result with the wrong tool_call id. What happens?
options: The provider or the model ignores the result and may call the tool again
why: Tool results must carry the matching call id. A mismatch drops the observation from the loop.

q: Arguments pass the JSON schema (amount is a number) but the unit is 'rupees' and the ledger expects cents. What check is missing?
options: Prompt-only unit hints with no code check
Business validation in code before the side effect — schema-valid is not business-valid
why: Types are not units or permissions. Validate ids and units in application code before you charge anyone.

q: You rewrite a tool description to be vaguer so it 'covers more cases'. Selection quality drops. Why?
options: Tool descriptions are context the model uses to choose; vague copy makes twins of every other tool
Descriptions are never sent to the model
Only the function name is read
why: Descriptions sit in the prompt and drive selection. Tighten them until a stranger could implement the tool.

q: Intent is one of three known tickets: refund, status, or cancel. Why is a routing table better than an agent loop?
options: A documented if/else over intent is easier to test than a free loop
Agents are required once you have three intents
why: A short, stable graph stays a workflow. An agent is for unknown graphs, not a 3-way switch.

q: You fan-out two lookups and one returns empty/failed. What must the join do?
options: Treat empty as success and continue
Handle the failed branch explicitly — skip, default, or fail the merge — not silently drop it
why: Fan-in is where empty branches become wrong answers. The join is a first-class step.

q: Why must a user-facing chat turn stay on the online path even if you have a batch API?
options: Batch APIs have multi-hour latency and no per-turn timeout you can show a user
why: Overnight evals use batch. Interactive turns need an online call with a timeout the user can feel.

q: You must fire 1000 independent classify calls without getting banned. Which trio belongs in the design?
options: Unlimited gather, no backoff, no alarm
One sync loop and no budget
A shared API key in the browser
A concurrency cap, jittered backoff, and a budget/rate alarm
why: That is the interview line: cap in-flight calls, back off with jitter, and page when the spend or 429 rate jumps.

q: A cheaper fallback model starts returning prose instead of your JSON schema during an outage. What was missing?
options: The same output contract (schema/tool) on the fallback as on the primary
why: A fallback that does not preserve the contract is a second incident. Same schema, same tool loop.

q: The LLM call succeeded but the tool HTTP timed out. Where does reliability logic still need to run?
options: Nowhere — tool failures are the model's problem
At the tool/API layer too: timeout, retry map, and an error result back to the model
why: Failures exist at both levels. A perfect chat completion with a dead tool is still a failed turn.

q: Tokens per request quietly triple after a prompt change. The process is healthy. What alert was missing?
options: A cost/token-per-request anomaly alert, not only process-death alerts
An alert on CSS bundle size
why: LLM bills die from tokens, not from crashed processes. Page when usage per request jumps.

q: You sum prompt plus completion tokens and call that the invoice. Why is that often wrong?
options: Cached, reasoning, or tool tokens and price tiers can differ from a raw sum
Only completion tokens ever cost money
why: Copy billed fields from the vendor when they exist. A naive sum misses cache discounts and extra billable channels.

q: LangChain is convenient in the capstone. How do you keep it from becoming the domain?
options: Put provider calls behind a thin port so you can replace the orchestrator
Store the chain object in the database
why: A thin orchestrator you can replace is the adult choice. LangChain is one approach, not the business logic.

q: What is the minimum end-to-end test of the streamed tool path?
options: A live billed call every CI minute
Fake the model, assert the tool ran with checked args, and that the UI received streamed tokens
why: CI should not need a vendor. Fake the model; assert the tool side effect and the stream the user would see.
